title: Chapter 8 Mastery Quiz: Statistical Inference & The Replication Crisis
description: Master NHST logic, Type I/II errors, statistical power, effect size, p-hacking, and Open Science reforms.

questions.question: What is the primary conceptual role of the Null Hypothesis (H0) in Null Hypothesis Significance Testing?

options.text: It posits that there is no true effect, difference, or relationship in the population
It guarantees that the researcher's theory is correct
It is an unproven assumption that participants are lying
It specifies that the sample size is equal to zero

questions.explanation: The null hypothesis represents the baseline assumption of no effect, against which sample evidence is evaluated.

questions.question: What does a statistically significant result of p < 0.05 formally mean?

options.text: There is less than a 5% probability of observing data this extreme if the null hypothesis is true
There is a 95% chance that the researcher's theory has been completely proven
The effect size is massive and of critical clinical importance
Exactly 5% of participants failed the test

questions.explanation: A p-value is the probability of obtaining test results at least as extreme as the observed results, assuming the null hypothesis is correct.

questions.question: What is a Type I Error in statistical hypothesis testing?

options.text: Rejecting the null hypothesis when the null hypothesis is actually true (a False Positive)
Failing to reject the null hypothesis when a real effect exists (a False Negative)
Entering data into the wrong column of a spreadsheet
Running an experiment without IRB consent

questions.explanation: A Type I error occurs when a researcher claims a genuine effect exists when in reality the result was merely random noise (false positive).

questions.question: What Greek letter represents the probability of committing a Type I Error?

options.text: Alpha (α)
Beta (β)
Gamma (γ)
Theta (θ)

questions.explanation: Alpha (α), conventionally set to 0.05, defines the threshold probability of committing a Type I error.

questions.question: What is a Type II Error in statistical decision making?

options.text: Failing to reject the null hypothesis when a real, genuine effect actually exists in the population (a False Negative)
Rejecting a true null hypothesis
Publishing two papers with the same title
Having a sample size greater than 500

questions.explanation: A Type II error (false negative) occurs when an experiment fails to detect a true population effect, often due to small sample size or high noise.

questions.question: What is Statistical Power?

options.text: The probability of correctly rejecting the null hypothesis when a true effect actually exists (1 - Beta)
The speed of statistical computing hardware
The political influence of the psychology department
The standard deviation multiplied by the mean

questions.explanation: Statistical power (1 - β) is the sensitivity of an experiment to detect a real effect if it exists.

questions.question: What is the widely accepted benchmark for adequate statistical power in psychological research?

options.text: Power = 0.80 (80% power)
Power = 0.05 (5% power)
Power = 0.50 (50% power)
Power = 1.00 always

questions.explanation: Jacob Cohen established 0.80 (an 80% chance of detecting a true effect) as the standard target for statistical power.

questions.question: Why is Effect Size (e.g., Cohen's d) often considered more informative than a p-value alone?

options.text: Effect size quantifies the magnitude and practical importance of a phenomenon, independent of sample size
Effect size cannot be calculated mathematically
Effect size only applies to qualitative interviews
Effect size is required by local city laws

questions.explanation: A p-value is heavily influenced by sample size (huge samples make trivial differences statistically significant), whereas effect size reflects true magnitude.

questions.question: According to Jacob Cohen's conventions, what magnitude of Cohen's d represents a 'Medium' effect size?
questions.explanation: Cohen defined d = 0.20 as small, d = 0.50 as medium, and d = 0.80 as large.

questions.question: What was the landmark finding of the Open Science Collaboration's 2015 Reproducibility Project in Psychology?

options.text: Only about 36% to 39% of 100 replicated studies found statistically significant results consistent with the original published findings
Every single study was proven to be an intentional fabrication
Cognitive psychology has zero validity
100% of all published effects replicated with larger effect sizes

questions.explanation: The 2015 replication effort revealed that fewer than 40% of classic findings replicated, launching the modern Open Science reform era.

questions.question: What is 'p-hacking'?

options.text: Trying numerous flexible analytical choices (dropping conditions, testing covariates, removing outliers) until p drops below 0.05
Using a computer to hack into another university's database
Calculating the p-value by hand on graph paper
Setting alpha to 0.001

questions.explanation: p-hacking exploits researcher degrees of freedom by trying different post-hoc analysis options until an arbitrary p < 0.05 threshold is achieved.

questions.question: A researcher stops recruiting participants the exact afternoon their data reaches p = 0.048, but would have continued recruiting if it had been p = 0.08. What questionable practice is this?

options.text: Data peeking (Optional stopping)
Latin square counterbalancing
Stratified random sampling
Triangulation

questions.explanation: Optional stopping peeks at results repeatedly and halts data collection only when statistical significance is briefly reached, heavily exploiting chance.

questions.question: What does the acronym 'HARKing' stand for in research methodology?

options.text: Hypothesizing After the Results are Known
Hypothetical Analysis of Random Kinematics
High Accuracy Ratio Kinetics
Human Assessment Review Knowledge

questions.explanation: HARKing involves presenting a post-hoc, data-driven exploratory result as if it had been an a priori, theory-derived confirmatory hypothesis.

questions.question: What is the 'File Drawer Problem'?

options.text: Studies that find non-significant or null results are rarely published and sit hidden in researchers' desks, biasing published literature toward false positives
Running out of physical filing cabinet space in a psychology office
Losing original paper surveys in a flood
Using physical folders instead of digital cloud storage

questions.explanation: Publication bias against null results hides negative findings in file drawers, skewing meta-analyses and creating an illusion of robust effects.

questions.question: What is Study Preregistration?

options.text: Registering study hypotheses, sample sizes, exclusion criteria, and planned analyses in an immutable public registry prior to data collection
Registering for a college psychology course before classes start
Paying an entry fee to attend an academic conference
Sending participants an email reminder 24 hours before their appointment

questions.explanation: Preregistration freezes study plans in an immutable time-stamped registry before data collection, preventing p-hacking, HARKing, and outcome switching.

questions.question: In the 'Registered Reports' publishing model, when does Stage 1 peer review and in-principle acceptance occur?

options.text: Before any empirical data are collected
After all data are collected, analyzed, and published
Only when the p-value is less than 0.0001
Ten years after the study finishes

questions.explanation: Stage 1 peer review assesses the theoretical rationale and methodology before data collection; approved papers are guaranteed publication regardless of the final outcome.

questions.question: What is the key difference between a Direct Replication and a Conceptual Replication?

options.text: Direct replication repeats the original procedures and measures exactly; conceptual replication tests the same hypothesis using different operationalizations
Direct replication uses humans; conceptual replication uses animals
Direct replication is conducted in a lab; conceptual replication is conducted in dreams
There is no difference; they are exact synonyms

questions.explanation: Direct replications verify if original findings can be reproduced with identical protocols; conceptual replications test generalizability across different methods.

questions.question: What is a 'Preprint' in modern psychological science?

options.text: A publicly accessible manuscript posted to an open digital repository (like PsyArXiv) before or during formal peer review
A preliminary receipt printed by a cash register
A rejected manuscript that can never be published
A handwritten draft from the 19th century

questions.explanation: Preprints provide free, rapid open access to scientific findings before commercial journal publication, accelerating scholarly exchange.

questions.question: What is the primary benefit of Open Data and Open Code practices in psychology?

options.text: Independent researchers can verify calculations, detect errors, and easily reproduce findings
It eliminates the need to teach statistics in universities
It guarantees that all future studies will find significant p-values
It allows commercial tech companies to sell participant personal identities

questions.explanation: Open data and analysis code ensure transparency, enabling peer audits, computational reproducibility, and seamless meta-analytic synthesis.

questions.question: What statistical visual plot is used in meta-analyses to detect publication bias by looking for an asymmetrical scattering of studies?

options.text: Funnel Plot
Pie chart
Venn diagram
Interaction line plot

questions.explanation: Funnel plots graph study effect sizes against standard error; missing chunks on the null side reveal publication bias.

questions.question: What is the 'Psychological Science Accelerator' (PSA)?

options.text: A globally distributed network of hundreds of laboratories that pool resources to run massive, highly powered multi-site replication and discovery studies
A machine that speeds up cognitive reaction time using electricity
A software program that automatically writes literature reviews
A financial grant offered only to Ivy League universities

questions.explanation: The PSA is a collaborative 'CERN for psychology' that coordinates hundreds of global labs to conduct massive, culturally diverse, high-powered studies.

questions.question: Why is the distinction between 'Confirmatory' and 'Exploratory' research essential to preserving scientific integrity?

options.text: Confirmatory research tests a priori hypotheses where p-values are valid; exploratory research generates new hypotheses from data patterns where traditional NHST p-values are not valid without independent verification
Confirmatory research is done on humans; exploratory research is done on computers
Exploratory research is strictly prohibited by the American Psychological Association
Confirmatory research never uses statistics

questions.explanation: Testing an a priori prediction provides a genuine test of a theory; hunting through data post-hoc generates hypotheses that must be confirmed on fresh, independent samples.
